chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL
(Written in shorthand.)

3 May. Bistritz.—I left Munich at 8:35 P. M. on 1 May and reached Vienna early the following morning. We were due at 6:46, but the train arrived an hour late. From what I could see through the train window, and during my short walk through its streets, Buda-Pesth looks a wonderful place. I dared not venture far from the station: we had arrived late, and the train would leave as close to its proper time as it could. I had the feeling that we were leaving the West behind and entering the East. The westernmost of the magnificent bridges across the Danube, a river impressively wide and deep here, carried us into a world shaped by the traditions of Turkish rule.

We left reasonably promptly and reached Klausenburgh after dark. I spent the night there at the Hotel Royale. For dinner—or rather supper—I had chicken prepared in some way with red pepper. It tasted very good, but made me thirsty. (Note: get the recipe for Mina.) When I asked the waiter about it, he called it “paprika hendl.” It was a national dish, he said, so I ought to find it anywhere along the Carpathians. The little German I know proved very useful here. In fact, I have no idea how I would manage without it.

While I had some free time in London, I went to the British Museum and searched the library’s books and maps for information about Transylvania. It occurred to me that knowing something about the country beforehand would surely help in my dealings with one of its noblemen. I find that the district he named lies in the far east of the country, where three states meet: Transylvania, Moldavia and Bukovina. It is in the heart of the Carpathian mountains, among the wildest and least-known regions of Europe. I could find no map or book showing the precise location of Castle Dracula. There are no maps of this country yet that can compare with our own Ordnance Survey maps. Bistritz, however, the postal town Count Dracula named, seems to be fairly well known. I shall copy some of my notes here; they may help me remember things when I tell Mina about my travels.

Transylvania’s population consists of four distinct nationalities. In the South are Saxons, and among them the Wallachs, descendants of the Dacians; in the West, Magyars; and in the East and North, Szekelys. It is among this last people that I am going. They say they descend from Attila and the Huns. This may be true: when the Magyars conquered the country in the eleventh century, they found the Huns already settled there. I have read that every superstition known to the world has gathered in the horseshoe formed by the Carpathians, as though this were the centre of a kind of whirlpool of the imagination. If that is so, my stay could be very interesting. (Note: I must ask the Count all about them.)

Despite a comfortable enough bed, I slept badly and had all sorts of strange dreams. A dog howled beneath my window throughout the night, which might explain it. Or perhaps it was the paprika: I drank every drop in my carafe and still felt thirsty. I fell asleep towards morning and woke to persistent knocking at the door, so I suppose by then I must have been sleeping deeply. Breakfast brought more paprika, a kind of maize-flour porridge they called “mamaliga,” and aubergine stuffed with minced meat, a particularly good dish called “impletata.” (Note: get that recipe too.) I had to rush through breakfast because the train left shortly before eight—or was supposed to. After hurrying to the station at 7:30, I sat in the carriage for over an hour before we moved. It seems the farther east one travels, the less punctual the trains become. What can they be like in China?

We seemed to crawl all day through a landscape rich in every kind of beauty. At times we saw little towns or castles perched on steep hilltops, like the pictures in old prayer books. At others we passed rivers and streams whose broad, stony banks on either side suggested heavy flooding. It takes a great quantity of fast-flowing water to scour the outer banks of a river bare. Every station had groups of people, sometimes whole crowds, dressed in all manner of clothes. Some looked just like peasants at home, or those I had seen while travelling through France and Germany: short jackets, round hats, and homemade trousers. Others were remarkably picturesque. The women looked pretty until one came close, but their waists were very bulky. All wore some sort of full white sleeves, and most had broad belts hung with strips of material that fluttered like a ballet costume, though of course they wore petticoats underneath. The strangest people we saw were the Slovaks, more barbarous in appearance than the others. They had large cowboy hats, enormous baggy trousers of a dirty white, white linen shirts, and heavy leather belts almost a foot wide, covered with brass studs. Their trousers were tucked into high boots; their hair was long and black, and their black moustaches thick. They make a striking picture, but hardly an inviting one. On a stage, anyone would immediately take them for an ancient band of Oriental brigands. Yet I am told they are quite harmless, and rather lacking in natural assertiveness.

Twilight was nearly gone when we arrived in Bistritz, a very interesting old town. It stands virtually on the frontier, since the Borgo Pass leads from it into Bukovina. Its history has accordingly been turbulent, and the traces are plain to see. Fifty years ago, a succession of great fires devastated it on five separate occasions. Early in the seventeenth century it endured a three-week siege in which 13,000 people died, famine and disease adding to the losses caused directly by the fighting.

Count Dracula had told me to stay at the Golden Krone Hotel. To my great delight, I found it thoroughly old-fashioned: naturally, I wanted to see as much as possible of the country’s ways. They were plainly expecting me. As I approached the entrance, a cheerful-looking elderly woman appeared in the usual peasant dress: a white undergarment and a long double apron, front and back, of coloured material that fitted almost too tightly for modesty. When I reached her, she bowed. “The Herr Englishman?” “Yes,” I answered, “Jonathan Harker.” With a smile, she said something to an elderly man in white shirt-sleeves who had followed her to the door. He went away and immediately returned carrying a letter:—

“My Friend.—Welcome to the Carpathians. I await your arrival with great eagerness. Sleep well tonight. Tomorrow at three the stagecoach leaves for Bukovina, and a seat has been reserved for you. My carriage will meet you at the Borgo Pass and bring you on to me. I hope your journey from London has been pleasant, and that you will enjoy your visit to my beautiful country.
“Your friend,
“DRACULA.”

4 May.—I discovered that my landlord had received a letter from the Count instructing him to reserve the best seat on the coach for me. But when I asked for details, he grew rather guarded and pretended not to understand my German. That could not be true: until then he had understood me perfectly—or at any rate had answered my questions exactly as though he did. He and his wife, the elderly woman who had welcomed me, exchanged frightened looks. He muttered that the money had come with a letter, and that he knew nothing more. I asked whether he knew Count Dracula and could tell me anything about the castle. Both husband and wife crossed themselves, said they knew absolutely nothing, and refused to speak further. Departure was so close that I had no time to question anyone else. It was all deeply mysterious, and far from reassuring.
Just as I was preparing to leave, the old woman came up to my room and spoke in a state of near hysteria:

“Do you have to go? Oh! young Herr, must you really go?” She was so agitated that she seemed to have forgotten much of her German, mixing it with another language I did not understand at all. Only by asking question after question could I just follow her. I explained that I must leave immediately, because I had important business to attend to. Then she asked me:
“Do you know what day this is?” I told her it was 4 May. Shaking her head, she repeated her question:
“Oh, yes! I know that! I know that—but do you know what day it is?” When I said I did not understand her meaning, she continued:

“It is the eve of St. George’s Day. Don’t you know that tonight, when the clock strikes twelve, every evil thing in the world will have its way? Do you know where you are going, and what you are going to?” She was so obviously distressed that I tried to reassure her, but nothing helped. At last she dropped to her knees and begged me not to go—or at least to postpone my departure for a day or two. It was all quite ridiculous, yet I felt uneasy. Still, I had business to carry out and could let nothing interfere. I tried to help her up and told her as seriously as I could that I was grateful, but my duty allowed no choice: I had to go. She stood up, wiped her eyes, and took a crucifix from her neck to offer me. I did not know how to respond. As a member of the Church of England, I had been taught to regard such things as somewhat idolatrous. Yet refusing an old woman who meant so well, and was so upset, seemed terribly unkind. She must have seen the hesitation on my face. She put the rosary around my neck herself, said, “For your mother’s sake,” and left the room. I am writing this part of my diary as I wait for the coach—which is late, naturally—and the crucifix is still around my neck. I cannot say whether it is the old woman’s terror, the many ghostly traditions here, or the crucifix itself, but my mind is much less at ease than usual. If this book ever reaches Mina before I do, let it carry my farewell. Here is the coach!

5 May. The Castle.—The grey dawn has passed, and the sun stands high above the far horizon. Its outline looks jagged, though whether from trees or hills I cannot tell: at that distance, large things and small blend together. I do not feel sleepy. Since no one is to call me until I wake, I am naturally writing until sleep comes. There are many peculiar things to record. In case anyone reading this imagines that I indulged too freely at dinner before leaving Bistritz, I shall set down exactly what I ate. It was something called “robber steak”: pieces of bacon, onion and beef, seasoned with red pepper, threaded on sticks and roasted over a fire, in the simple style of meat sold for London cats! The wine was Golden Mediasch. It gives a curious, though not unpleasant, sting to the tongue. I had only two glasses, and nothing else to drink.

When I climbed into the coach, the driver had not yet taken his place; I saw him in conversation with the landlady. They were clearly discussing me, for they kept glancing in my direction. Some people sitting on the bench outside the door—a bench whose local name means “word-bearer”—came over to listen, and then looked at me too, most of them with pity. Many words kept recurring, strange words, for the crowd contained people of several nationalities. Quietly, I took my multilingual dictionary from my bag and looked them up. They did nothing to encourage me. Among them were “Ordog”—Satan; “pokol”—hell; “stregoica”—witch; and “vrolok” and “vlkoslak,” which both mean the same thing, one in Slovak and the other in Servian: a creature that is either a werewolf or a vampire. (Note: I must ask the Count about these superstitions.)

As we set off, the crowd outside the inn, now quite large, all crossed themselves and pointed two fingers at me. I had some trouble persuading a fellow passenger to explain these gestures. At first he would not answer, but when he learned I was English, he said they were a charm or protection against the evil eye. This was hardly pleasant, as I was setting out for a place I did not know to meet a man I had never seen. Yet everyone seemed so kind, so sad and so full of sympathy that I could not help being moved. I shall never forget my last view of the inn-yard: those picturesque figures standing around the broad archway, all making the sign of the cross, with the rich leaves of oleanders and orange trees behind them, clustered in green tubs in the middle of the yard. Then our driver cracked his great whip over the four little horses harnessed abreast, and we began our journey. His wide linen trousers—“gotza,” they call them—spread across the whole front of the driver’s seat.

As we drove on, the beauty around us soon made me forget my ghostly fears. Had I understood the language—or rather the languages—of the other passengers, perhaps I could not have shaken them off so readily. Ahead stretched green, sloping country, thick with forests and woods. Here and there, steep hills carried clumps of trees or farmhouses with their windowless gable ends facing the road. Fruit blossom was everywhere in a dazzling profusion: apple, plum, pear and cherry. Passing the trees, I could see fallen petals scattered like stars across the green grass beneath them. The road wound among these green hills, which they call the “Mittel Land,” disappearing around a grassy curve or behind the ragged edges of pine woods that ran down the hillsides like tongues of flame. The surface was rough, yet we seemed to race over it in a fever of haste. I did not then understand the hurry, but the driver plainly meant to reach Borgo Prund without wasting a moment. I was told that the road is excellent in summer, but had not yet been repaired after the winter snow. In that respect it differs from most Carpathian roads: an old tradition says they must not be kept in too good a condition. The Hospadars of former times refused to repair them, for fear the Turk would think they were preparing to admit foreign troops. That might bring forward the war which was, in truth, always ready to break out.

Beyond the green, rounded hills of the Mittel Land, enormous wooded slopes climbed towards the lofty heights of the Carpathians themselves. They towered on both sides of us. The full afternoon sunlight revealed all the magnificent colours of this beautiful range: deep blue and purple in the shadows beneath the peaks, green and brown where grass met rock, and jagged rocks and pointed crags stretching away in an endless succession until they vanished in the distance, where snowy summits rose in splendour. Here and there the mountains seemed split by vast clefts. As the sun began to set, these openings gave us occasional glimpses of the white flash of falling water. We rounded the foot of a hill, and a high, snow-covered mountain peak came into view. One of my companions touched my arm. As our twisting route carried us on, the peak seemed to stand directly ahead:—
“Look! Isten szek!”—“God’s seat!”—he said, reverently making the sign of the cross.

Our winding journey seemed endless. The sun sank lower behind us, and evening shadows began creeping around us. They seemed darker because the snowy mountaintop still caught the sunset and glowed a delicate, cool pink. We passed Cszeks and Slovaks here and there, all in picturesque clothes, though I noticed how distressingly common goitre was among them. Crosses stood all along the roadside, and my companions crossed themselves as we sped past. Occasionally a peasant man or woman knelt before a shrine without even turning at our approach. So complete was their absorption in worship that they seemed blind and deaf to the world outside it. I saw many things unfamiliar to me: haystacks set among the trees, for instance, and beautiful groups of weeping birches, their white trunks shining like silver through the delicate green leaves. Every so often we passed a leiter-wagon, the usual peasant cart, with its long, snakelike backbone designed to follow the uneven road. It invariably carried a group of peasants on their way home. The Cszeks wore white sheepskins, the Slovaks coloured ones; the latter held their long staffs, each ending in an axe, upright like lances. As night approached it grew bitterly cold. In the deepening twilight, the shadows of oak, beech and pine seemed to melt together into one dark haze. But as we climbed through the Pass, dark firs sometimes stood out against lingering snow in the deep valleys between the projecting hills. At times the road cut through pine woods that appeared to close over us in the darkness. Great patches of grey, scattered here and there among the trees, gave the scene a strangely eerie and solemn air. They prolonged the grim imaginings that had begun earlier that evening, when the setting sun threw into startling relief those ghostly clouds which seem always to be winding through the Carpathian valleys. Some hills were so steep that the horses could only climb slowly, however much our driver hurried them. I wanted to get out and walk uphill, as we do at home, but he would not allow it. “No, no,” he said. “You mustn’t walk here; the dogs are too savage.” Then, plainly attempting a grim joke—for he looked around for the others’ approving smiles—he added, “And you may have quite enough of that sort of thing before you get to sleep.” He stopped only long enough to light his lamps.

Once darkness fell, the passengers became visibly excited. One after another they spoke to the driver, apparently pressing him to go faster still. He flogged the horses mercilessly with his long whip, urging them to greater efforts with wild shouts. Ahead, I could make out a patch of grey light in the darkness, as though the hills were divided by a gap. The passengers grew even more agitated. Our rickety coach rocked on its great leather springs, pitching like a boat on a stormy sea, and I had to cling on. The road levelled out, and we seemed to fly. Then the mountains on either side appeared to close in and glare down at us: we were entering the Borgo Pass. Several passengers offered me gifts, one after another, insisting so earnestly that refusal was impossible. The gifts were certainly strange and varied, but each was offered with simple sincerity, a kind word and a blessing. With them came the same curious gestures of fear I had seen outside the Bistritz hotel: the sign of the cross and the protection against the evil eye. As we raced along, the driver bent forward, and passengers on both sides leaned out over the coach’s edge, straining to see into the dark. Clearly something intensely exciting was either happening or expected. I questioned every passenger, but not one would give me any explanation at all. Their excitement lasted for some time. Eventually we saw the eastern side of the Pass opening before us. Dark clouds rolled overhead, and the air felt heavy and oppressive with approaching thunder. It was as though the mountain range divided two different atmospheres and we had now entered the stormy one. By this time I too was watching for the carriage that would take me to the Count. At every moment I expected lamps to shine through the blackness, but everything remained dark. Our own lamps supplied the only light, flickering through the white cloud of steam rising from our hard-driven horses. The sandy road lay pale before us, with no vehicle anywhere in sight. The passengers settled back with a relieved sigh that seemed to mock my disappointment. I had begun considering what to do when the driver glanced at his watch and said something to the others so quietly that I barely caught it. I thought he said, “An hour before the time.” Turning to me, he spoke in German even worse than mine:—

“There is no carriage. The Herr is not expected after all. He will come on to Bukovina now and return tomorrow or the day after. Better the day after.” As he spoke, the horses started neighing, snorting and plunging wildly, forcing him to restrain them. Then, amid screams from the peasants and a general making of the sign of the cross, a four-horse calèche came up from behind, passed us and stopped beside the coach. Our lamps flashed across the horses: magnificent creatures, black as coal. Their driver was a tall man with a long brown beard and a large black hat that seemed to conceal his face. When he turned towards us, all I could make out was a pair of intensely bright eyes, looking red in the lamplight. He addressed our driver:—
“You have arrived early tonight, my friend.” The coachman stammered his answer:—
“The English Herr wanted to hurry.” The stranger answered:—

“That must be why you wanted him to continue to Bukovina, I suppose. You cannot trick me, my friend. I know too much, and my horses are fast.” He smiled as he spoke. In the lamplight I saw a hard mouth, very red lips and teeth that looked sharp and white as ivory. One passenger whispered to another a line from Burger’s “Lenore”:—
“Denn die Todten reiten schnell”— (“For the dead travel fast.”)

The unfamiliar driver evidently caught the words, for he looked up with a brilliant smile. The passenger turned away, extending two fingers and crossing himself at the same time. “Give me the Herr’s luggage,” the driver said. My bags were passed out and placed in the calèche with extraordinary speed. It had stopped close beside us, so I climbed down from the side of the coach. The driver helped me, seizing my arm in a grip like steel; he must have possessed tremendous strength. Without speaking, he shook the reins. The horses turned, and we swept into the darkness of the Pass. Looking back, I saw steam rising from the coach horses in the lamplight, with the figures of my former companions outlined against it as they crossed themselves. Their driver cracked his whip, shouted to his horses, and they raced away towards Bukovina. As they vanished into the dark, a strange chill and a feeling of loneliness came over me. But a cloak was laid over my shoulders and a rug over my knees, and my driver spoke in excellent German:—

“It is a cold night, mein Herr, and my master, the Count, told me to take every care of you. There is a flask of slivovitz—the local plum brandy—under the seat, should you want it.” I drank none, though knowing it was there was comforting all the same. I felt distinctly strange, and considerably frightened. I think I would have chosen any available alternative to continuing that night journey into the unknown. The carriage sped straight ahead; then we turned completely around and travelled along another straight road. I had the impression that we were covering the same ground again and again. I watched for a recognisable landmark and confirmed that we were. I wanted to ask the driver what it meant, but truly I was afraid to. In my position, I thought, any protest would be useless if someone intended to delay me. After a while I grew curious about the time, struck a match and held its light to my watch. It was only a few minutes before midnight. That startled me: I suppose my recent experiences had strengthened the common superstitions about that hour. I waited, sick with suspense.

A dog began howling somewhere at a farmhouse far along the road: a long, agonised wail that sounded full of fear. Another dog answered, then another and another. The wind was now sighing gently through the Pass, carrying a wild chorus of howls that seemed to rise from the whole countryside, as far as my imagination could reach into the dark. At the first cry, the horses strained and reared. The driver spoke soothingly, and they settled, though still trembling and sweating as if they had just bolted in a sudden panic. Then a louder, sharper howling began far away in the mountains on either side: wolves. The horses and I reacted alike. I wanted to leap out of the calèche and run; they reared again and plunged so madly that the driver needed all his immense strength to stop them bolting. Within a few minutes, however, I grew used to the sound, and the horses calmed enough for the driver to climb down and stand before them. He stroked and soothed them, whispering into their ears as horse-tamers are said to do. The effect was extraordinary. Under his touch they became quite manageable, though they still shook. He returned to his seat, shook the reins and drove off at a great speed. This time, after reaching the far side of the Pass, he abruptly turned into a narrow road branching sharply to the right.

Soon trees surrounded us, sometimes arching completely over the road so that we seemed to pass through a tunnel. Elsewhere great, forbidding rocks rose like guards on either side. Though we were sheltered, we heard the strengthening wind moan and whistle among the rocks, while branches crashed together overhead as we raced past. It grew colder and colder. Fine, powdery snow began falling, and soon a white blanket covered both us and everything around us. The cutting wind still brought the dogs’ howls, growing fainter as we travelled. The wolves’ cries, however, drew steadily nearer, as though they were closing in from every direction. I became terribly afraid, and the horses shared my terror. The driver alone remained quite undisturbed. He kept turning his head from side to side, but in the darkness I could see nothing.

Suddenly I noticed a faint blue flame flickering some distance to our left. The driver saw it at the same instant. He immediately reined in the horses, jumped down and disappeared into the dark. I had no idea what to do, especially as the wolves’ cries were coming closer. While I was wondering, he abruptly reappeared, took his seat without speaking, and drove on. I think I must have fallen asleep and repeatedly dreamed the same incident, for it seemed to happen over and over without end. Looking back now, it has the quality of a dreadful nightmare. Once the flame appeared so close to the road that even in the surrounding darkness I could follow the driver’s movements. He hurried to the spot where the blue light rose. It must have been extremely faint, since it did not seem to light the ground around it at all. He gathered a few stones and arranged them in a pattern. At one point there was a strange trick of vision: when he stood between me and the flame, he did not block it. I could still see its ghostly flicker through him. This startled me, but it lasted only a moment, so I assumed my eyes had deceived me as I strained to see in the dark. For a while after that, no blue flames appeared. We sped through the blackness, surrounded by the wolves’ howling as though they were following us in a travelling circle.

At last the driver went farther from the carriage than he had gone before. While he was away, the horses began shaking more violently than ever, snorting and screaming in fear. I could see no reason for it: the wolves had stopped howling altogether. Just then the moon sailed out through the black clouds, appearing behind the jagged crest of an overhanging rock covered in pines. Its light revealed a ring of wolves surrounding us. They had white teeth, dangling red tongues, long sinewy limbs and shaggy coats. In that grim silence they were a hundred times more terrifying than they had been when howling. I felt almost paralysed with fear. Only when a man finds himself face to face with such horrors can he understand what they really mean.

Without warning the wolves began howling again, as if the moonlight had affected them in some strange way. The horses plunged and reared, looking helplessly around with eyes that rolled so desperately it hurt to watch. But the living ring of terror enclosed them on every side, and there was no escape. I called for the driver. Our only chance, it seemed to me, was to try to break through that ring and help him reach us. I shouted and hammered the side of the calèche, hoping the noise would drive back the wolves on that side and leave him a way to the carriage. I have no idea how he got there, but suddenly I heard his voice lifted in a tone of absolute command. Turning towards it, I saw him standing in the road. He swept his long arms through the air as though clearing away some invisible obstruction, and the wolves retreated, farther and farther. At that moment a heavy cloud covered the moon, plunging us into darkness again.

When I could see once more, the driver was climbing into the calèche and the wolves were gone. Everything was so strange and unnatural that a terrible fear seized me; I dared neither speak nor move. Time seemed without end as we drove on, now in almost total darkness, with rolling clouds hiding the moon. We continued climbing, broken occasionally by a swift descent, but always going higher overall. Suddenly I realised that the driver was bringing the horses to a halt in the courtyard of an enormous ruined castle. Not a single ray of light showed in its tall black windows, and its broken battlements cut a jagged outline against the moonlit sky.

chapters.title: Chapter II
paragraphs: JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL—continued

5 May.—I must have fallen asleep. Surely, if I had been fully awake, I would have noticed our approach to such an extraordinary place. The courtyard looked quite large in the darkness. Several dark passages led away from it beneath huge rounded arches, which may have made it seem larger than it is. I have not yet had a chance to see it in daylight.

As soon as the calèche stopped, the driver sprang down and offered his hand to help me out. Once more I could not help noticing his tremendous strength. His hand really felt like a steel vice, capable of crushing mine if he wished. He lifted out my luggage and set it beside me on the ground. I was standing by an enormous old door studded with large iron nails, set into a projecting entrance of massive stone. Even in the weak light I could see the bold carving on the stonework, though age and weather had worn it badly. While I stood there, the driver climbed back into his seat and shook the reins. The horses moved forward, and the whole carriage disappeared into one of the dark passageways.

I remained where I was, silent, with no idea what to do. There was neither bell nor knocker. It seemed unlikely that my voice could carry through those forbidding walls and dark window openings. The wait felt endless, and doubts and fears crowded into my mind. What was this place, and what kind of people lived here? What grim adventure had I stumbled into? Was this an ordinary part of a solicitor’s clerk’s life, sent abroad to explain the purchase of a London estate to a foreign client? A solicitor’s clerk! Mina would object to that. A solicitor—for just before leaving London I learned that I had passed my examination. I am now a fully qualified solicitor! I rubbed my eyes and pinched myself to check whether I was awake. Everything seemed a dreadful nightmare. I expected to wake suddenly in my own home, with dawn struggling through the windows, as I sometimes have after overworking the day before. But I felt the pinch, and there was no mistaking what my eyes saw. I was awake, and I was in the Carpathians. All I could do was be patient and wait for morning.

Just as I reached this conclusion, heavy footsteps approached from behind the great door, and a moving light shone through its cracks. Chains rattled and enormous bolts clanged as they were drawn back. A key turned with the loud, scraping sound of a lock long unused. Then the great door swung open.

Inside stood a tall old man, clean-shaven except for a long white moustache. He wore black from head to foot, without a trace of colour anywhere. In one hand he carried an antique silver lamp. Its flame had no glass chimney or globe around it, and as the draught from the open doorway made it flicker, long shadows trembled across the walls. With his right hand the old man courteously gestured for me to enter. He spoke excellent English, though with a peculiar intonation:—

“Welcome to my home! Enter freely, and by your own choice!” He did not step forward to meet me. Instead he stood motionless as a statue, as if the welcoming gesture had turned him to stone. But the moment I crossed the threshold, he moved quickly towards me and held out his hand. His grip was so powerful that it made me wince, and its icy coldness did nothing to lessen the effect. It felt more like a dead man’s hand than a living one. Again he spoke:—

“Welcome to my home. Come freely. Leave in safety, and leave behind some of the happiness you bring!” His handshake was so like the driver’s in its strength that for a moment I wondered whether I was speaking to the same man. I had not seen the driver’s face. To make certain, I asked:—
“Count Dracula?” He gave a courtly bow before answering:—

“I am Dracula, and I welcome you to my home, Mr. Harker. Come inside. The night air is cold, and you must be in need of food and rest.” While speaking, he set the lamp on a wall bracket, stepped outside and picked up my luggage. Before I could stop him he had carried it in. I protested, but he would not listen:—

“No, sir. You are my guest. The hour is late, and my servants are unavailable. Allow me to attend to your comfort myself.” He insisted on taking my bags along the passage, up a great spiral staircase and through another broad corridor, where our footsteps echoed heavily on the stone floor. At its end he opened a heavy door. To my delight, it revealed a brightly lit room with a table set for supper and a huge hearth where newly added logs blazed and crackled.

The Count stopped, set down my bags and closed the door. Crossing the room, he opened another door into a small eight-sided chamber. A single lamp lit it, and it seemed to have no window at all. He went through it, opened yet another door and invited me to enter. What a welcome sight: a large, well-lit bedroom, warmed by another log fire. This too had been replenished recently, for the logs on top were fresh. A hollow roar rose from it up the wide chimney. The Count put my luggage inside himself, then withdrew. Before closing the door he said:—
“After your journey, you will want to wash and make yourself comfortable. I hope you will find everything you need. When you are ready, return to the other room. Your supper will be waiting there.”

The warmth, the light and the Count’s polite welcome seemed to drive away all my fears and doubts. Once I felt myself again, I realised I was almost starving. I washed and tidied myself as quickly as possible, then went into the other room.
Supper was already laid out and waiting for me. My host stood beside the great fireplace, leaning against its stonework. With an elegant gesture towards the table, he said:—
“Please sit down and eat as much as you wish. I hope you will forgive me for not joining you. I have already had dinner, and I do not take supper.”

I gave him the sealed letter Mr. Hawkins had entrusted to me. He opened it and read it with a serious expression. Then, smiling most pleasantly, he passed it back for me to read. At least one passage filled me with delight.

“I regret that an attack of gout, a complaint from which I suffer continually, makes it quite impossible for me to travel for some time. I am pleased, however, to be able to send a capable replacement in whom I have complete confidence. He is a young man of energy, with considerable talents of his own and an extremely loyal nature. He is discreet, knows when to hold his tongue, and has grown to manhood while in my service. Throughout his stay he will be at your disposal whenever you require him, and will follow your instructions in every matter.”

The Count came over himself and lifted the cover from a serving dish. I immediately began eating an excellent roast chicken. My supper consisted of this, some cheese and salad, and a bottle of old Tokay, of which I drank two glasses. As I ate, the Count questioned me about my journey, and little by little I told him everything that had happened.

When supper was over, my host asked me to draw a chair up to the fire. He offered me a cigar, explaining that he did not smoke himself, and I began to smoke it. This gave me a chance to look at him more closely. His features were extraordinarily distinctive.

His face had a pronounced—indeed, a very pronounced—aquiline cast. His narrow nose had a high bridge and strangely arched nostrils, beneath a high, domed forehead. His hair was sparse at the temples but thick elsewhere. His eyebrows were extremely heavy, nearly joining above his nose, their bushy hairs seeming to curl from sheer abundance. What I could see of his mouth under the thick moustache looked set and rather cruel. Unusually sharp white teeth projected over his lips, whose remarkable redness suggested astonishing vitality in a man so old. His ears were pale and sharply pointed at the tips; his chin was broad and powerful, his cheeks thin but firm. Above all, he gave an impression of extraordinary paleness.

Until then I had only noticed the backs of his hands, resting on his knees in the firelight, and they had appeared rather white and delicate. Now that they were close to me, I could see that they were actually coarse and broad, with short, thick fingers. Strangely, hair grew in the middle of his palms. His nails were long and fine, filed to sharp points. When he leaned over me and touched me with his hands, I could not stop myself shuddering. Perhaps it was the foulness of his breath, but a horrible nausea swept over me, and however hard I tried, I could not hide it. The Count evidently noticed. He drew back with a grim smile that exposed his jutting teeth more clearly than before, then sat down again on his own side of the hearth. Neither of us spoke for a while. Glancing towards the window, I saw the first faint streak of approaching dawn. A strange stillness seemed to rest over everything. Yet when I listened, I heard many wolves howling, apparently far below in the valley. The Count’s eyes shone as he said:—
“Hear them—the children of the night. What music they make!” He must have seen something in my expression that puzzled him, for he added:—
“Ah, sir, those of you who live in cities cannot understand a hunter’s feelings.” He stood up and continued:—

“But you must be weary. Your bedroom is ready, and tomorrow you may sleep for as long as you please. I must be away until afternoon. Sleep well, and may your dreams be pleasant!” With a courteous bow he personally opened the door into the eight-sided room for me, and I went through to my bedroom....
I feel adrift in a sea of wonders. I am full of doubt and fear; strange thoughts come to me that I dare not admit even to myself. May God protect me, if only for the sake of those I love!

7 May.—It is early morning once more, but the past twenty-four hours have brought rest and enjoyment. I slept far into the day and woke naturally. After dressing, I went into the room where we had eaten supper. A cold breakfast was set out, and a pot of coffee stood on the hearth to keep hot. A card on the table read:—

“I must be away for a little while. Please do not wait for me.—D.” I sat down and thoroughly enjoyed a substantial meal. Afterwards I searched for a bell to tell the servants I had finished, but there was none. The house certainly lacks some odd things, considering the extraordinary wealth evident all around me. The tableware is gold, so beautifully made that it must be immensely valuable. The curtains, the fabrics covering chairs and sofas, and the hangings around my bed are of the richest, most beautiful materials. They must have cost a fortune when new; they are centuries old, though perfectly preserved. I saw similar things at Hampton Court, but those were worn, frayed and moth-eaten. Yet not one of these rooms contains a mirror. There is not even a dressing mirror on my table. Before I could shave or brush my hair I had to unpack my little shaving glass. I have neither seen a servant anywhere nor heard any sound around the castle apart from wolves howling. Some time after my meal—I hardly know whether to call it breakfast or dinner, since I ate between five and six—I began looking for something to read. I did not want to wander through the castle without first asking the Count’s permission. The room held absolutely nothing: no book, no newspaper, not even writing materials. I opened another door and found what seemed to be a library. I also tried the door opposite my own, but it was locked.

To my great pleasure, the library contained an enormous collection of English books, filling whole shelves, along with bound magazines and newspapers. More English magazines and newspapers lay scattered on a table in the centre, though none were very recent. The books covered every sort of subject: history, geography, politics, economics, botany, geology and law. All concerned England, its life, customs and manners. There were even reference works: the London Directory, the “Red” and “Blue” books, Whitaker’s Almanac, the Army and Navy Lists, and—somehow its presence cheered my heart—the Law List.
While I was examining the books, the door opened and the Count came in. He greeted me warmly and hoped I had slept well. Then he continued:—

“I am pleased you have discovered this room. I am certain you will find much here to interest you. These companions”—he rested a hand on several books—“have been faithful friends. For some years now, ever since I first thought of going to London, they have given me many, many happy hours. Through them I have learned to know your great England, and to know her is to love her. I long to walk the crowded streets of your mighty London, to stand amid the rush and whirl of humanity and share in its life, its changes, its death—everything that makes it what it is. Alas, though! Until now I have learned your language only from books. I depend on you, my friend, to teach me how to speak it.”
“But, Count,” I replied, “you understand and speak English perfectly well!” He bowed solemnly.

“Thank you, my friend. Your opinion is far too flattering. I fear I have travelled only a short distance along the road I wish to follow. Yes, I know the vocabulary and the grammar; but I have yet to learn how to speak the language.”
“Really,” I told him, “your spoken English is excellent.”

“It is not,” he replied. “I know very well that if I walked and spoke in London, everyone would immediately recognise a foreigner. That will not satisfy me. Here I am a nobleman, a boyar. The common people know who I am, and I am their master. But a stranger in a strange country is nobody. People do not know him, and what they do not know, they do not care about. I shall be content when I am like everyone else: when no one stops at the sight of me or breaks off a conversation on hearing my voice to say, ‘Ha, ha! A foreigner!’ I have been master for so long that I wish to remain master—or at least to have no one else as master over me. You have come for more than explaining my new London estate as the representative of my friend Peter Hawkins of Exeter. I hope you will stay here with me for a while. Through our conversations I can learn English intonation, and I ask you to point out every mistake I make in speaking, however small. I regret being away for so much of today, but I know you will forgive a man with so many important matters to attend to.”
Naturally, I assured him as warmly as I could that I would be willing. I also asked whether I might use this room whenever I wished. “Yes, certainly,” he replied, adding:—

“You are free to go anywhere in the castle except through locked doors, where of course you would not wish to enter. Everything is as it is for a reason. If you could see through my eyes and know what I know, perhaps you would understand better.” I assured him that I was certain of it. Then he continued:—

“We are in Transylvania, and Transylvania is not England. Our customs differ from yours, and you will find many things strange. Indeed, from what you have already told me of your experiences, you have some idea of the strange things you may encounter.”

This started a long conversation. He clearly wanted to talk, even if only for the pleasure of talking, so I asked many questions about things I had seen or experienced. Sometimes he avoided a subject or shifted the conversation by pretending not to understand. Mostly, however, he answered my questions with great frankness. As time passed I grew a little bolder and asked about some of the previous night’s odd happenings—for example, why the driver had visited the places where the blue flames appeared. He explained a common belief: on one particular night each year—last night, in fact, when all evil spirits are believed to roam unchecked—a blue flame appears wherever treasure lies hidden. “There can be little doubt,” he continued, “that treasure is buried in the country you crossed last night. For centuries the Wallachian, the Saxon and the Turk fought over that ground. There is scarcely a foot of soil in the whole region that has not been enriched with human blood, whether of patriots or invaders. Those were turbulent days, when Austrians and Hungarians advanced in hordes and the people went out to defend their country: women and men, old people and children alike. They waited on the rocks above the passes and brought destruction down on the enemy in avalanches of their own making. When an invader conquered, he found almost nothing. Everything of value had been entrusted to the friendly earth.”

“But how,” I asked, “can it have stayed hidden so long, when there is a reliable sign to show anyone who takes the trouble to look?” The Count smiled. His lips drew back over his gums, revealing the long, sharp canine teeth in a peculiar way. He answered:—

“Because the peasant is a coward and a fool at heart! The flames appear on only one night, and on that night no man in this country will leave his house if he can possibly avoid it. And even if he did, my dear sir, he would not know what to do. Why, even that peasant you describe, who marked the spot where the flame appeared, would not know where to search by daylight for the work of his own hands. I dare say that even you could not find those places again?”
“You are right about that,” I said. “I have no more idea than the dead where to begin looking.” After that our conversation turned to other things.

“Come,” he said at last, “tell me about London and the house you have found for me.” Apologising for neglecting my duty, I went to my room to fetch the papers from my bag. As I sorted them, I heard china and silver rattling next door. Passing back through that room, I saw that the table had been cleared and the lamp lit: by now it had long been dark. Lamps were burning in the study, or library, too. I found the Count stretched on the sofa, reading, of all things, an English Bradshaw’s Guide. At my arrival he cleared books and papers from the table, and together we examined plans, deeds and figures of every kind. Everything interested him. He asked countless questions about the property and its surroundings. He had obviously read everything he could find about the neighbourhood beforehand, for by the end it was clear that he knew far more about it than I did. When I remarked on this, he replied:—

“But surely, my friend, I need to know these things? Once I am there I shall be alone. My friend Harker Jonathan—forgive me; I have followed my country’s custom of putting the family name first—my friend Jonathan Harker will not stand beside me to help me and correct my mistakes. He will be far away in Exeter, probably working on legal papers with my other friend, Peter Hawkins. So!”

We examined every detail of the purchase of the Purfleet estate. I explained the facts, obtained his signature on the necessary documents and wrote a letter to accompany them, ready for posting to Mr. Hawkins. Then he asked how I had found a property so well suited to his needs. I read him the notes I had made at the time, which I copy here:—

“In a side road at Purfleet I found a property that appeared to meet the requirements exactly. A battered notice announced that it was for sale. It is enclosed by a high, ancient wall of heavy stone, unrepaired for many years. The gates are shut: solid old oak and iron, with the iron badly eaten by rust.

“The estate is named Carfax, probably a corruption of the old Quatre Face: the house has four sides, aligned with the four cardinal points of the compass. About twenty acres in all lie within the solid stone wall already described. There are numerous trees, making parts of the grounds gloomy. A deep, dark-looking pond or small lake is apparently fed by springs, since its water is clear and runs off in a fairly large stream. The house is enormous, with parts from many periods going back, I would guess, to medieval times. One section has immensely thick stone walls, pierced by only a few high windows with heavy iron bars. It resembles part of a castle keep and stands close to an old chapel or church. I could not enter the chapel, since I lacked the key to the connecting door from the house, but I photographed it with my Kodak from several positions. The house has acquired additions in a very irregular way. I can only estimate how much ground it occupies, which must be considerable. There are few neighbouring houses. One is a very large building, recently extended and converted into a private lunatic asylum, though it cannot be seen from the grounds.”
When I finished reading, he said:—

“I am pleased it is large and old. My own family is ancient; living in a new house would be the death of me. A house cannot become fit to live in overnight. After all, how few days there are in a century. The ancient chapel pleases me too. We Transylvanian noblemen dislike the thought of our bones lying among the common dead. I am not seeking merriment or pleasure, or the bright sensual delights of abundant sunshine and sparkling water that appeal to the young and carefree. I am young no longer. Years of weary mourning for the dead have left my heart ill-suited to joy. Besides, my castle’s walls are crumbling. It has many shadows, and cold wind breathes through its broken battlements and windows. I love shade and darkness, and I wish to be alone with my thoughts whenever I can.” Somehow his expression did not match his words—or perhaps the shape of his face simply made his smile look sinister and malicious.

A little later he excused himself and left, asking me to gather my papers. He remained away for some time, and I started examining the books around me. One was an atlas. It fell open naturally at the map of England, as though that page had been consulted often. Small circles marked several places. Looking closely, I saw that one lay east of London, plainly marking his new estate. The other two were Exeter and Whitby, on the Yorkshire coast.

The Count returned after nearly an hour. “Aha!” he said. “Still studying your books? Good! But you must not work all the time. Come; I am told your supper is ready.” He took my arm and led me into the next room, where an excellent meal awaited me. Again he apologised for not eating: he had dined while he was out. As on the previous night, however, he sat with me and talked while I ate. Afterwards I smoked, again as before, while he remained beside me, chatting and asking questions on every imaginable subject, hour after hour. I felt it must be very late, but said nothing. I believed I ought to oblige my host in every possible way. Yesterday’s long sleep had refreshed me, so I was not drowsy, yet I could not escape that chill which comes over one as dawn approaches—a change something like the turning tide. They say people close to death usually die as dawn comes or the tide turns. Anyone who has felt that change in the air while exhausted and bound, as it were, to a post of duty can readily believe it. Suddenly a cock crowed, its call reaching us with an unnaturally piercing clarity through the clear morning air. Count Dracula leapt to his feet and said:—

“Why, morning has come again! How careless of me to keep you awake so long. You must make your accounts of my dear new country, England, less fascinating, so that I do not forget how swiftly the hours pass.” With a courteous bow, he hurried from the room.

Back in my bedroom I opened the curtains, but there was little to see. The window faced the courtyard, and my only view was of the warming grey of the brightening sky. I closed the curtains once more and have written down the events of the day.

8 May.—While writing in this book, I had begun to worry that I was rambling too much. Now I am glad I recorded everything in detail from the beginning. There is something so strange about this place and everything in it that I cannot feel at ease. I wish I were safely away—or had never come at all. Perhaps this strange habit of living through the night is affecting me, but if only that were the whole explanation! I could endure it if I had someone to talk to. There is nobody. My only companion in conversation is the Count, and he!—I fear I may be the only living soul here. Let me keep to plain facts as far as I can. It will help me hold steady. I must not let my imagination run wild; if I do, I am lost. Let me state my situation at once—or what it seems to be.

After going to bed I slept only a few hours. Feeling unable to sleep longer, I got up. I had hung my shaving mirror beside the window and was just starting to shave when a hand suddenly touched my shoulder and I heard the Count say, “Good morning.” I jumped. How had I failed to see him? The mirror reflected the whole room behind me. My sudden movement gave me a small cut, though I did not notice it just then. I answered his greeting and looked into the glass again to discover how I had been mistaken. This time there could be no doubt: he stood close behind me, where I could see him over my shoulder. But the mirror showed no reflection of him! The entire room was visible, yet there was no sign of any man in it but myself. It was startling. Coming after so many other odd events, it deepened the vague uneasiness I always feel near the Count. At that instant, though, I noticed that my cut was bleeding a little, and blood was running down my chin. I put down the razor and half turned to look for sticking plaster. When the Count saw my face, his eyes flared with a kind of demonic rage. Suddenly he lunged for my throat. I pulled away, and his hand struck the string of beads carrying the crucifix. The change was immediate. His fury vanished so quickly that I could scarcely believe I had seen it.

“Be careful,” he said. “Be careful when you cut yourself. In this country it is more dangerous than you imagine.” He seized the shaving mirror and continued: “And here is the miserable object that caused the trouble. A vile trinket of human vanity. Away with it!” With one wrench of that terrible hand he pulled open the heavy window and hurled the mirror out. It smashed into a thousand pieces on the courtyard stones far below. He left without another word. This is extremely inconvenient. I cannot see how I shall shave now, except by using my watch-case or the bottom of my shaving-pot, which is fortunately metal.

Breakfast was ready when I entered the dining room, but I could find the Count nowhere, so I ate by myself. How strange that I have still never seen him eat or drink. He must be a most peculiar man! Afterwards I explored a little of the castle. Going out onto the stairs, I found a room facing South. The view was magnificent, and my position gave me every chance to appreciate it. The castle stands on the very brink of a terrifying precipice. A stone dropped from the window would fall a thousand feet without striking anything! Green treetops stretch like a sea as far as the eye can reach, broken now and then by a deep cleft marking a chasm. Here and there silver threads show where rivers wind through the forest in deep ravines.

But I have no heart to describe beautiful scenery. After looking out, I explored farther and found doors, doors, doors on every side—all locked and bolted. There is no way out anywhere, except through the windows in the castle walls.
This castle is a prison in every sense, and I am its prisoner!

chapters.title: Chapter III
paragraphs: JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL—continued

When I realised I was a prisoner, a kind of frenzy seized me. I ran up and down the stairs, tried every door and looked out of every window I could reach. Before long, though, the certainty that I was helpless overwhelmed every other feeling. Looking back a few hours later, I think I must have temporarily lost my mind: I behaved like a rat in a trap. But once I accepted my helplessness, I sat down quietly—as quietly as I have ever done anything—and began considering what I should do. I am still thinking, without reaching any firm conclusion. There is only one thing I know for certain: telling the Count what I think would be useless. He knows perfectly well that I am imprisoned. He has confined me himself, and undoubtedly has reasons of his own. If I told him openly what I had discovered, he would only deceive me. As far as I can see, my sole course is to keep my knowledge and my fears to myself, and watch carefully. Either my fears are fooling me like a child, or I am in desperate danger. If it is the latter, I need every ounce of intelligence I have, now and in the days ahead, to survive.

Scarcely had I decided this when I heard the great door downstairs close and knew the Count had returned. He did not come straight to the library. I crept carefully to my bedroom and found him making the bed. It was strange, but confirmed what I had suspected all along: there were no servants here. Later, through a crack beside the door hinges, I saw him setting the dining-room table. That settled it. Surely, if he performs all these humble duties himself, there can be nobody else to do them. The thought frightened me. If no one else is in the castle, then the Count must have driven the carriage that brought me here. What a terrible idea! If so, what does it mean that he could control those wolves merely by silently raising his hand? Why were the people at Bistritz and on the coach so terribly afraid for me? What did their gifts mean—the crucifix, the garlic, the wild rose, the mountain ash? Bless that good, good woman who put the crucifix around my neck! Whenever I touch it, it gives me strength and comfort. How odd that something I was taught to disapprove of as idolatrous should help me in this lonely, troubled state. Does something in the object itself have this power? Or is it a means of recalling sympathy and comfort, a physical thing that helps bring those memories back? One day, if I can, I must examine this question and decide what I think. For now I must learn everything possible about Count Dracula; it may help me understand. Perhaps tonight I can steer the conversation towards himself and persuade him to talk. But I must take great care not to arouse his suspicion.

Midnight.—I have talked with the Count at length. A few questions about Transylvanian history brought him wonderfully to life. He spoke of events and people, especially battles, as though he had witnessed every one. Afterwards he explained that a boyar takes the pride of his family and name as his own: their glory is his glory, their fate his fate. When speaking of his family he always said “we,” almost using the royal plural. I wish I could reproduce everything exactly as he said it, for I found it fascinating. It seemed to contain the country’s entire history. As he talked he became excited, pacing the room, tugging at his long white moustache and gripping whatever came to hand as if to crush it by sheer force. I shall record one speech as closely as I can, for in its own way it tells the story of his people:—

“We Szekelys have every right to pride. The blood in our veins comes from many brave peoples who fought like lions for mastery. Here, in this whirlpool of European races, the Ugric tribe brought down from Iceland the fighting spirit bestowed by Thor and Wodin. Their Berserkers unleashed it with such deadly purpose on the coasts of Europe—yes, and Asia and Africa too—that people believed the werewolves themselves had arrived. When they came here, they found the Huns, whose fury in battle had swept across the earth like a living fire. Dying nations believed that the Huns carried the blood of ancient witches, driven from Scythia, who had coupled with devils in the desert. Fools, fools! What witch or devil ever matched Attila, whose blood runs in these very veins?” He raised his arms. “Is it surprising that we conquered, that we were proud, that we drove back the Magyar, the Lombard, the Avar, the Bulgar and the Turk when they poured thousands of men across our borders? Is it strange that Arpad and his legions, sweeping through the Hungarian homeland, found us already here when they reached the frontier, and that the Honfoglalas was completed there? When that Hungarian flood swept east, the victorious Magyars recognised the Szekelys as their kin. For centuries they entrusted us with guarding the border of Turkey-land. Yes, and beyond that, with the never-ending duty of frontier watch, for as the Turks say, ‘water sleeps, and enemy is sleepless.’ Who among the Four Nations received the ‘bloody sword’ more eagerly than we, or answered its call to war by gathering more swiftly beneath the King’s standard? When was our nation’s great disgrace avenged—the shame of Cassova, when the banners of Wallach and Magyar fell before the Crescent? Who but a man of my own blood, as Voivode, crossed the Danube and defeated the Turk on his own soil? There was a true Dracula! What sorrow that after his fall his own unworthy brother sold his people to the Turk and brought the disgrace of slavery upon them! Surely it was this Dracula who inspired another of his line in a later age to lead his armies again and again across the great river into Turkey-land. Driven back, he returned again, and again, and again—even when he had to come away alone from a field drenched in blood, where his soldiers were being slaughtered. He knew that only he could win in the end! They said he cared for nobody but himself. Bah! What use are peasants with no leader? How can a war be won without a mind and a heart to direct it? Later, after the battle of Mohács, when we cast off Hungarian rule, men of Dracula’s blood were among the leaders. Our spirit could not endure the loss of freedom. Ah, young sir, the Szekelys—with the Draculas as their lifeblood, their brains and their swords—have a history that upstart families like the Hapsburgs and Romanoffs can never equal. The days of war have passed. Blood is considered too precious in these times of dishonourable peace, and the glory of the great races is nothing more than a story told.”

Morning was approaching by then, and we went to bed. (Note: this diary is becoming horribly like the opening of the “Arabian Nights,” since everything must break off at cockcrow—or like the ghost of Hamlet’s father.)

12 May.—I shall start with facts: plain, scanty facts, confirmed by books and figures, beyond all doubt. I must keep them separate from experiences for which I have only my own observation, or my memory of it. When the Count emerged from his room yesterday evening, he began questioning me about legal matters and the way certain kinds of business are conducted. I had spent a weary day with the books. Simply to occupy my mind, I had reviewed some matters I studied at Lincoln’s Inn. There was a definite pattern to the Count’s questions, so I will try to record them in order. The information might help me somehow, at some future time.

His first question was whether someone in England could employ two or more solicitors. I said he could employ a dozen if he liked, but that engaging several for a single transaction would be unwise. Only one could act at any given time, and changing solicitors would certainly work against his interests. He seemed to understand completely. Next he asked whether there would be any practical obstacle to employing one solicitor for, say, banking and another for shipping, if he needed local assistance somewhere far from the banking solicitor’s home. I requested a fuller explanation so that I would not accidentally give him misleading advice. He said:—

“Let me give an example. Our mutual friend Mr. Peter Hawkins, working in the shadow of your beautiful Exeter cathedral, a long way from London, buys my London property for me through you. Very good! Now, I should explain frankly why I chose someone so far from London instead of a man who lived there, in case you find it strange. I wanted no local interest to be served: only my wishes. A London resident might have interests of his own or a friend’s to promote. So I looked farther away for an agent who would work for my interests alone. Suppose now that, having many affairs to manage, I wish to send goods to Newcastle, Durham, Harwich or Dover. Would it not be easier to consign them to someone in those ports?” I told him that would certainly be straightforward. However, solicitors have a system of acting as agents for one another. Any solicitor can instruct a local colleague to handle local work. A client need only place his affairs with one man, who can then carry out his wishes without troubling him further.
“But,” he asked, “I would still be free to give those instructions myself, would I not?”
“Certainly,” I replied. “This is often done by businessmen who prefer that no single person should know the full extent of their affairs.”

“Good!” he said. He then asked how consignments were arranged, what formal procedures must be followed, and what difficulties might arise that careful planning beforehand could prevent. I explained all these matters as fully as I was able. He certainly left me feeling that he would have made a remarkable solicitor, for there seemed to be nothing he had failed to consider or anticipate. For a man who had never visited the country, and who apparently did very little business, his knowledge and practical insight were extraordinary. When he had satisfied himself on every point he had raised, and I had checked all of them as thoroughly as possible against the books available, he suddenly stood up and asked:—

“Since your first letter, have you written again to our friend Mr. Peter Hawkins, or to anyone else?” With some bitterness I answered that I had not. So far, I had seen no opportunity to send a letter to anybody.

“Then write now, my young friend,” he said, resting a heavy hand on my shoulder. “Write to our friend and to anyone else you wish. You may tell them, if you please, that you will remain with me for another month.”
“Do you want me to stay that long?” I asked, the thought chilling my heart.

“Very much indeed. In fact, I shall accept no refusal. When your master, employer—whatever you call him—undertook to send someone to represent him, it was understood that my requirements alone were to govern the arrangement. I have spared no expense. Is that not so?”

What could I do except bow my agreement? It was Mr. Hawkins’s business, not mine; I had to consider his interests before my own. Besides, something in Count Dracula’s eyes and manner as he spoke reminded me that I was a prisoner. However much I might wish otherwise, I had no choice. He saw his victory in my bow and his power over me in my troubled face. He immediately began taking advantage of both, in that smooth, irresistible manner of his:—

“My dear young friend, I ask that you confine your letters to business matters. Your friends will surely be glad to hear you are well and looking forward to returning home to them. Will they not?” As he spoke, he gave me three sheets of paper and three envelopes, all made of the thinnest material used for foreign post. I looked at them, then at him. His quiet smile showed the sharp canine teeth resting over his red lower lip. I understood as clearly as if he had told me outright: I must watch what I wrote, because he would be able to read it. I decided to write only formal notes for now, and secretly compose a full account for Mr. Hawkins later. I would write to Mina too, using shorthand, which would puzzle the Count even if he found it. After finishing my two letters, I sat quietly with a book while he wrote several notes of his own, consulting books on his table as he worked. Then he placed my letters with his, put away his writing things and left. The instant the door closed, I leaned over to inspect the letters lying face down on the table. I felt no guilt. In these circumstances, I believed I should protect myself by every means available.

One letter was addressed to Samuel F. Billington, No. 7, The Crescent, Whitby; another to Herr Leutner, Varna; the third to Coutts & Co., London; and the fourth to Herren Klopstock & Billreuth, bankers, Buda-Pesth. The second and fourth were not sealed. I was about to examine them when the door handle moved. I dropped back into my chair, having barely enough time to put the letters exactly as they had been and pick up my book. The Count entered carrying yet another letter. He gathered those on the table, carefully put stamps on them, then turned to me:—
“Please forgive me, but I have a great deal of private work to attend to tonight. I hope you will find everything to your liking.” At the doorway he turned back, paused, and said:—

“Let me offer you advice, my dear young friend—no, let me give you a most serious warning. If you leave these rooms, you must on no account fall asleep elsewhere in the castle. It is ancient and holds many memories. Those who choose unwisely where to sleep may have bad dreams. Take heed! If sleep overtakes you now or at any other time, or you feel it approaching, hurry to your own bedroom or return here. Your rest will then be safe. But if you fail to take this care, then—” He ended with a dreadful gesture, moving his hands as though washing them. I understood perfectly. My only uncertainty was whether any dream could be worse than the unnatural, horrible web of darkness and mystery closing around me.

Later.—I stand by what I wrote last, but this time there is no room for doubt. I will not be afraid to sleep anywhere that he is absent. I have hung the crucifix above the head of my bed. I imagine that it makes my sleep less troubled by dreams, and there it will stay.

After he left, I went to my bedroom. Some time passed without a sound, so I came out and climbed the stone stairs to the place from which I could look South. Although I could not reach that vast landscape, it offered a sense of freedom compared with the courtyard’s cramped darkness. Looking out, I felt all the more that I was in prison and longed for a breath of fresh air, even night air. This nocturnal life is beginning to affect me. My nerves are failing. I jump at my own shadow, and my mind teems with dreadful imaginings. God knows there is enough in this accursed place to justify my terror! The beautiful expanse before me lay bathed in soft yellow moonlight, almost bright as day. Distant hills melted into that gentle light, while the valleys and gorges held shadows of velvety black. The beauty alone seemed to lift my spirits. Each breath brought peace and comfort. As I leaned out, a movement caught my eye a storey below and a little to the left. Judging from the arrangement of the rooms, I thought the Count’s own windows must be there. My window was tall and deeply recessed, divided by stone mullions. Though weathered, the stonework was intact, but the window’s frame had plainly been missing for many years. I withdrew behind the stone and cautiously peered out.

It was the Count’s head emerging from a window. I could not see his face, but recognised his neck and the movements of his back and arms. In any case, there was no mistaking the hands I had studied so often. At first I watched with interest and even a little amusement. It is extraordinary how small a thing can interest and amuse a prisoner. But those feelings turned to disgust and terror as his whole body slowly came through the window and began crawling down the castle wall above that dreadful gulf, face downwards, his cloak spread around him like enormous wings. At first I refused to believe what I saw. Surely it was some trick of moonlight, some strange play of shadows. I kept watching, though, and there could be no mistake. His fingers and toes gripped the corners of stones where years of weathering had worn away the mortar. Using every jutting edge and uneven surface, he moved rapidly downwards, just as a lizard moves along a wall.

What kind of man is this—or what creature has taken a man’s appearance? The horror of this place is overwhelming me. I am afraid—terribly afraid—and there is no escape. Terrors surround me that I dare not even think about....

15 May.—Again I have seen the Count leave in his lizard-like way. He crawled diagonally downwards, about a hundred feet below and well to the left, then vanished into a hole or window. After his head disappeared, I leaned out to see more, without success. He was too far away for me to obtain the right angle. Knowing that he had now left the castle, I decided to explore more boldly than I had dared before. I returned to the room, fetched a lamp and tried every door. All were locked, as expected, and the locks were fairly new. I went down the stone staircase to the hall through which I had first entered. The bolts slid back readily enough and I could undo the great chains, but the door was locked, and there was no key! The key must be in the Count’s room. I must watch for a chance when his door is unlocked, so that I can take it and escape. I continued my thorough examination of the stairways and passages, trying every door along them. One or two small rooms by the hall were open, but contained nothing except old, moth-eaten furniture thick with dust. At last, at the top of a staircase, I found a door that seemed locked but yielded slightly when pushed. I pressed harder. It was not actually locked: its hinges had sagged, leaving the heavy door dragging on the floor. Here was a chance that might not come again. With repeated efforts I forced it back far enough to enter. I stood in a wing farther to the right than the rooms I knew, and one storey lower. From the windows I saw that this suite extended along the castle’s southern side. The end room had windows facing both West and South. A great precipice lay on each side. The castle stood at the corner of a huge rock, making it unassailable on three sides. Here they had put great windows out of reach of sling, bow or culverin cannon, securing a light and comfort impossible in rooms that had to be defended. To the West stretched a broad valley. Far beyond it rose jagged mountain strongholds, peak after peak, their sheer rock dotted with mountain ash and thorn rooted in cracks and crevices. Clearly this was where the ladies had lived in former times: the furniture looked more comfortable than any I had yet seen. No curtains covered the windows. Yellow moonlight poured through the diamond-shaped panes, bright enough to reveal colours while softening the thick coating of dust and partly concealing the damage done by time and moths. My lamp added little to the brilliant moonlight, but I was glad to have it. The place had a terrifying loneliness that chilled my heart and set my nerves trembling. Even so, it was better than being alone in the rooms I had grown to hate through the Count’s presence. After making an effort to steady myself, I felt a gentle calm settle over me. Here I sit at a little oak table, where perhaps some beautiful lady once composed a badly spelt love letter with much deliberation and blushing, recording in shorthand everything that has happened since I last closed my diary. This is the up-to-date nineteenth century with a vengeance. Yet unless my senses are deceiving me, the old centuries possessed, and still possess, powers of their own that mere “modernity” cannot destroy.

Later: the morning of 16 May.—God keep me sane, for that is all I have left to ask. Safety, and even the belief in safety, belong to the past. As long as I remain here, my only hope is that I shall not go mad—if I am not mad already. If I am still sane, surely the thought alone could drive me out of my mind: of all the foul things hiding in this hateful place, the Count now terrifies me least. Only he can keep me safe, and only while I remain useful to him. Great God! Merciful God! I must be calm; losing my calm truly leads to madness. I am beginning to understand certain things that have puzzled me. Until now, I never fully grasped what Shakespeare meant when he made Hamlet say:—
“My tablets! quick, my tablets! ’Tis meet that I put it down,” etc.,

for now, feeling that my own mind has come unhinged, or has received the shock that must eventually destroy it, I seek comfort in my diary. The habit of recording things accurately must help quiet my thoughts.

The Count’s mysterious warning frightened me when he gave it. Remembering it now frightens me still more, because from this point on he has a terrible power over me. I shall be afraid to question anything he says!

After writing my diary—and fortunately putting the book and pen back into my pocket—I grew drowsy. I remembered the Count’s warning, but took pleasure in defying it. Sleep was approaching, accompanied by the stubbornness that so often comes ahead of it. The gentle moonlight soothed me; the wide landscape outside offered a refreshing sense of freedom. I decided not to go back that night to those rooms haunted by darkness, but to sleep here. In earlier days, ladies had sat here singing and living gentle lives, their tender hearts grieving for the men away in merciless wars. I pulled a large couch away from its place near a corner, arranging it so that I could look out while lying down at the beautiful view to East and South. Without thinking or caring about the dust, I settled myself to sleep. I suppose I must have slept. I hope I did, but I am afraid: everything that followed was startlingly real. So real that now, sitting here in the full bright morning sunshine, I cannot bring myself to believe it was only a dream.

I was not alone. Nothing in the room had changed since I entered. In the bright moonlight I could see my own footprints across the floor, where I had disturbed years of accumulated dust. Facing me in that light stood three young women, ladies by their clothing and bearing. At the time I thought I must be dreaming, because although the moon shone behind them, they cast no shadows on the floor. They approached, studied me for a while and whispered to one another. Two were dark, with high, hooked noses like the Count’s and large, piercing dark eyes that appeared almost red against the pale yellow moonlight. The third was fair—as fair as anyone could be—with great waves of golden hair and eyes like pale sapphires. Somehow I thought I recognised her face, associated with a dreamlike terror, but I could not recall where or how I had seen it. All three had dazzling white teeth, shining like pearls against their full, ruby-red lips. Something about them troubled me, stirring both desire and a deadly fear. Deep in my heart I felt a wicked, burning wish to be kissed by those red lips. I should not write this, in case Mina someday reads it and is hurt; but it is true. They whispered together, then all three laughed. Their laughter was silver and musical, yet so hard that it seemed impossible for such sounds to have passed through soft human lips. It resembled the unbearably sweet, tingling notes of water-glasses played by a skilled hand. The fair girl shook her head flirtatiously while the other two encouraged her. One said:—
“Go on! You are first; we will come after you. You have the right to begin.” The other added:—

“He is young and strong. There are kisses enough for all of us.” I lay still, watching beneath my eyelashes in an agony of pleasurable expectation. The fair girl came forward and leaned over me until I felt her breath moving against me. In one way it was sweet, sweet as honey, sending the same tingling through my nerves as her voice. But beneath that sweetness was something bitter and repellent, like the smell of blood.

I dared not lift my eyelids, though I could see perfectly beneath my lashes. She knelt beside me and bent over me, openly savouring the sight. Her deliberate sensuality thrilled and disgusted me at once. Arching her neck, she actually licked her lips like an animal. In the moonlight I could see moisture shining on those scarlet lips and on the red tongue moving over sharp white teeth. Her head sank lower and lower. Her lips passed below my mouth and chin, seeming about to close on my throat. Then she stopped. I heard the wet movement of her tongue licking teeth and lips, and felt her hot breath on my neck. The skin of my throat began tingling, as skin does when a hand about to tickle it draws closer and closer. Her lips touched that exquisitely sensitive skin, soft and trembling. I felt the hard pressure of two pointed teeth, barely touching, pausing there. I closed my eyes in a languid ecstasy and waited—waited, my heart pounding.

At that instant another sensation flashed through me like lightning. I knew the Count was there, surrounded, it seemed, by a storm of rage. My eyes opened without my willing them to. His powerful hand seized the fair woman’s slender neck and pulled her back with a giant’s strength. Fury transformed her blue eyes; her white teeth snapped in anger and her pale cheeks burned red with passion. But the Count! I had never imagined such wrath, even in the demons of hell. His eyes actually blazed. A lurid red light shone from them, as though hellfire burned behind them. His face was deathly white, its lines rigid as drawn wires. The heavy eyebrows joining above his nose looked like a shifting bar of white-hot metal. With a violent sweep of his arm he flung the woman away. Then he gestured at the others as if beating them back—the same commanding movement I had seen him use with the wolves. His voice was low, almost a whisper, yet it seemed to slice through the air and ring around the room:—

“How dare any of you touch him? How dare you even look at him when I forbade it? Back, all of you, I say! This man is mine! Take care how you interfere with him, or you will answer to me.” The fair girl turned to reply with a laugh of coarse flirtation:—

“You have never loved anyone yourself. You never love!” The other women joined her. Their hard, empty, joyless laughter rang through the room until I almost fainted at the sound. It seemed the delight of devils. After studying my face closely, the Count turned and answered in a soft whisper:—

“Yes, I too am capable of love. You yourselves know that from the past, do you not? Well, I promise you this: when I have finished with him, you may kiss him as much as you wish. Now go! Go! I must wake him; we have work to do.”

“Are we to get nothing tonight?” one of them asked with a quiet laugh. She pointed to the bag he had thrown on the floor, which was moving as though something alive lay inside. He answered with a nod. One woman sprang forward and opened it. Unless my ears deceived me, I heard a gasp and a faint cry, like a child half suffocated. The women gathered around it while I watched, appalled. Then, before my eyes, they disappeared, taking the dreadful bag with them. There was no doorway nearby, and they could not have passed me unseen. They seemed simply to melt into the moonbeams and drift through the window. For an instant I saw their dim, shadowy shapes outside before they faded altogether.
Then the terror was too much for me, and I collapsed unconscious.
